title: Closer to AI, Easier to Replace?
text: If AI can perform more of a job’s tasks, it seems natural to expect fewer workers to be needed. Yet AI might also help workers produce more, making their skills more valuable. So this article explores whether a job’s closer connection to AI means a greater risk of replacement.

title: Closer to AI, Easier to Replace?
section: How do we measure the connection to AI?
text:
How do we measure the connection to AI?
Anthropic’s Economic Index maps observed Claude usage to work tasks and occupations. The BLS Employment Projections database provides U.S. employment by occupation in 2024 and projected employment in 2034. Python joins them using Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) codes; an occupation such as accounting can span many industries.
AI exposure summarizes observed AI use across occupational tasks, accounting for factors such as task time and usage patterns. Task breadth is the share of matched tasks with positive AI penetration, counting each task equally. Neither measures the probability that a worker will lose their job.
The matched sample contains 722 occupations, retaining those with at least 95% task matching against O*NET 30.0 task descriptions. The vertical axis measures projected employment growth. It provides an employment outlook, not an observed AI replacement rate.




Explore: hover for employment and sample coverage; click a group to see its occupations. Search for one occupation to isolate it, then clear the search to restore the group. Switch the horizontal axis to compare exposure with task breadth.
Group exposure and breadth use 2024 employment weights. Bubble area represents sample employment; group growth uses summed employment. Hover shows sample coverage relative to the official group. Detailed dots are equal-sized so smaller occupations remain visible.

title: Closer to AI, Easier to Replace?
section: Does closer AI exposure mean more replacement?
text:
Does closer AI exposure mean more replacement?
Similar AI exposure can accompany very different employment outlooks. In the group view, compare business and financial operations with sales: their exposure is almost the same, at 28.8% and 27.5%, yet projected employment grows 5.2% in business/finance and falls 2.6% in sales. Their bubbles sit close together horizontally but on opposite sides of zero growth.
Computer and mathematical occupations provide a second comparison. Their exposure is 35.3%, slightly higher than the 33.9% for office and administrative support. Yet computer/math employment is projected to grow 10.0%, while office support declines 3.9%. The more exposed group has the stronger outlook, which challenges the simple expectation that closer contact with AI necessarily means fewer jobs.
These are comparisons of the matched occupations within each group, not every job in the economy. They show why exposure alone is insufficient to judge an occupation’s outlook. They cannot tell us how much employment would grow without AI, or how many workers AI might replace within a growing group.

title: Closer to AI, Easier to Replace?
section: Does broader task coverage mean greater risk?
text:
Does broader task coverage mean greater risk?
The task-breadth view shows the same contrast: broad coverage can coexist with growth or decline. Switch the horizontal axis to task breadth. Business/finance and office support have nearly identical coverage, at 24.2% and 25.1%, but their growth projections remain +5.2% and −3.9%. Sales has somewhat narrower coverage (22.2%) and still declines, while computer/math has the broadest coverage of these four groups (34.1%) and the strongest growth (+10.0%).
For these groups, counting how widely AI appears across tasks does not resolve the difference in employment outlooks. Breadth counts tasks equally, regardless of their time requirements or importance, and does not distinguish assistance from replacement. Clicking a group and inspecting an occupation’s task panel helps readers see what lies behind its average, rather than treating all covered tasks as equivalent.

title: Closer to AI, Easier to Replace?
section: How might we explain the difference?
text:
How might we explain the difference?
AI may complement professional skills while replacing routine tasks. This offers one possible explanation for the contrast between office support and computer/math occupations. Automating repetitive clerical tasks, such as data entry and document processing, could reduce demand for some office-support roles. Meanwhile, wider AI adoption could increase demand for workers who develop software, integrate AI systems, and evaluate their outputs. AI could also help these workers spend more time on design and complex problem-solving. Both groups contain varied tasks and skill requirements; the chart is consistent with this explanation, but does not establish that AI causes either projection.
Demand may offset labor savings: cheaper software or advice could attract more customers, supporting employment despite lower labor requirements per service. Trust, accountability, and unusual cases may preserve human roles, while adoption costs delay substitution. These mechanisms could explain divergent outlooks, but these chart comparisons do not establish them; BLS projections incorporate forces beyond AI.

title: Closer to AI, Easier to Replace?
section: Takeaway
text:
Takeaway
A closer connection to AI does not consistently coincide with a weaker employment outlook. Business/finance and computer/math are projected to expand, while similarly exposed sales and office-support groups contract; switching to task breadth preserves this contrast. AI may save labor on some tasks while complementing skills or expanding demand elsewhere, so exposure need not translate directly into falling employment. For our own skill development and career choices, how AI penetrates specific tasks may matter more than whether a job is simply labeled “AI-exposed.” It is worth learning to use AI while strengthening judgment and interpersonal skills; exposure alone is not a reason to avoid an occupation.

Sources and replication. Anthropic supplies occupational exposure and task penetration; BLS supplies the archived 2024–2034 projections; O*NET supplies task descriptions. GitHub replication repository and downloadable files, including the source data, Python scripts, results, and README. All comparisons are descriptive and use the matched sample.

title: Low Taxes, Deep Pockets? Who Funds Your State?
text: Taxes vary widely across U.S. states and matter when choosing where to live. Higher taxes can support better public services, but do states that collect more tax really have richer governments? And what else decides how much money a state government has?

title: Low Taxes, Deep Pockets? Who Funds Your State?
section: How far apart are state tax bills?
text:
How far apart are state tax bills?
I use the U.S. Census Bureau’s Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances, combining state and local governments because states divide responsibilities differently. Taxes per person is their combined tax revenue divided by population, averaged over FY2022–2024. It measures collections per resident, not each resident’s tax bill.

The range is wide. DC collects $14,967 per resident, compared with under $5,000 in Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi. Higher collections cluster in the Northeast, California and Hawaii; lower collections extend across much of the South and interior West. Adjacent low-tax states form a broad southern belt rather than isolated exceptions. The pattern suggests regional differences in tax bases and fiscal choices, although the map alone cannot separate their effects.

title: Low Taxes, Deep Pockets? Who Funds Your State?
section: Does counting all revenue close the gap?
text:
Does counting all revenue close the gap?
Taxes are not a government’s only money. General revenue adds fees, tuition, interest, natural-resource royalties and federal transfers to taxes, excluding utility and pension-fund income. If these sources compensate low-tax states, the geographic gap should narrow.

General revenue ranges from $9,819 per person in Tennessee to $30,191 in DC. The gap barely narrows: the highest-to-lowest ratio remains 3.1, while the 90th-to-10th percentile ratio falls from 1.8 to 1.7.
On the map, the Southeast stays relatively light and the Northeast stays dark. The lower-revenue area stretches from Tennessee through Georgia and toward Florida, while California and Oregon remain comparatively well funded on the Pacific coast. Alaska, Wyoming and New Mexico stand out against this coastal pattern. Other income changes some states’ positions without erasing the broader regional divide. Darker colors everywhere partly reflect adding revenue sources; they do not by themselves show convergence.

The bars show why the gap persists: the ten highest-tax jurisdictions receive about $4,990 per person in federal transfers, versus $3,470 for the ten lowest. Federal transfers therefore do not offset the difference between these groups. This comparison describes funding patterns, not the causal effect of federal aid.
Alaska, Wyoming and New Mexico reach the top five in total revenue despite lower tax rankings. Their larger non-tax revenues raise another question: who actually pays the taxes they collect?

title: Low Taxes, Deep Pockets? Who Funds Your State?
section: Who actually pays the taxes?
text:
Who actually pays the taxes?
Taxes can fall on nonresidents, including visitors and customers buying goods produced elsewhere. I approximate their share by comparing Tax Foundation estimates of residents’ taxes paid to their own state with Census collections per resident in 2022. A 50% share means outsiders bear about half.


Connecticut’s −2% reflects differences between calendar-year estimates and fiscal-year collections, not an actual negative nonresident share.

The strongest nonresident shares lie in Alaska and a set of interior states: North Dakota, Wyoming and New Mexico. This is not a uniform western pattern: neighboring Idaho and Utah are blue, while Nevada is warmer. California and much of the Northeast also remain blue despite their relatively high tax collections. DC is a localized exception on the eastern seaboard. The geography of who pays differs from the geography of how much governments collect. Resource production offers one explanation for the interior hotspots; tourism and commuting offer others for Nevada and DC.

title: Low Taxes, Deep Pockets? Who Funds Your State?
section: What the map tells us
text:
What the map tells us
Across the three maps, much of the Northeast combines high tax collections with high revenue, while parts of the Southeast remain lower on both. Alaska and selected interior states break this pattern, combining strong revenues with high estimated nonresident shares.
Higher collections generally accompany better-funded governments, but local tax bills do not tell the whole story. Where a state sits—and the economic activities connected to that location—helps shape both its funding and who bears the cost. These maps reveal associations, not proof that geography causes fiscal outcomes.
Amounts are nominal, without cost-of-living adjustments; nonresident shares combine modeled estimates and fiscal-year collections for one year.

Sources and replication. U.S. Census government finances, population estimates and state boundaries; Tax Foundation’s 2022 state-local tax burdens. Data, R scripts and replication instructions are in the GitHub repository and README.

title: Tech Dominates the Forbes Rich List. Do Tech and Finance Careers Really Pay More?
text: The Forbes billionaires list highlights extraordinary wealth associated with technology companies. Finance also has a reputation for high pay. But billionaire wealth comes largely from ownership, while most career decisions concern wages. Do typical tech and finance workers earn more than people in other occupations? Is the advantage visible early in adulthood, and has it changed over time?

title: Tech Dominates the Forbes Rich List. Do Tech and Finance Careers Really Pay More?
section: From the survey to the comparison
text:
From the survey to the comparison
I use IPUMS CPS, drawing on the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) from survey years 1976–2025. Each survey asks about income in the preceding calendar year, so the earnings series runs from 1975 to 2024. The sample contains 2,191,970 person-year records after restricting to wage and salary workers ages 25–64 who usually worked at least 35 hours a week and at least 50 weeks in the previous year. A person appearing in multiple surveys contributes multiple records.
Earnings are annual pretax wages and salaries (INCWAGE). Occupations are based on the longest-held job in that income year (OCC10LY), harmonized to a 2010 classification. I group computing, software, information systems, and computer hardware jobs as Tech; financial management, accounting, analysis, advice, insurance, and related sales as Finance; healthcare management and clinical or technical jobs as Healthcare; and other identified civilian occupations as Other. Thus these are occupations, not employer industries. The Tech group captures many AI-related jobs but cannot identify every AI worker.
Each median uses the CPS ASEC person weight (ASECWT) to describe the represented population, rather than treating every survey respondent as equally representative. To compare dollar levels across years, I use IPUMS’s CPI factor to express them in 2024 dollars. The three-year age chart pools observations after this adjustment and divides each person’s weight by three.

title: Tech Dominates the Forbes Rich List. Do Tech and Finance Careers Really Pay More?
section: Which occupations pay more now?
text:
Which occupations pay more now?
For income earned in 2024, Tech’s weighted median was $116,000, followed by $98,000 in Finance, $81,120 in Healthcare, and $60,000 in Other. The 2024 estimates use 2,149 Tech and 1,722 Finance sample records. The boxplots put 2022–2024 incomes on a common 2024-dollar scale.



Weighted earnings distributions for four occupation groups in 2022–2024. Boxes show the 25th to 75th percentiles, center lines the medians, and whiskers the 10th to 90th percentiles.


Across all three years, the medians rank Tech, Finance, Healthcare, then Other. Tech stays near $116,000, while Finance rises each year from $85,725 to $98,000. Healthcare edges down; Other is roughly stable. Tech and Finance also have wider earnings distributions in dollar terms than Healthcare and Other, as shown by their larger interquartile ranges: in 2024, Tech’s middle half runs from $75,000 to $160,000, versus $41,600 to $95,000 for Other. Finance’s 90th percentile slightly exceeds Tech’s, despite its lower median; the distributions overlap.

title: Tech Dominates the Forbes Rich List. Do Tech and Finance Careers Really Pay More?
section: Is the gap present early?
text:
Is the gap present early?
Yes. Among respondents ages 25–29 in the pooled 2022–2024 data, Tech’s median was $96,441, Finance’s $77,260, and Other’s $50,363 in 2024 dollars. Tech leads at every plotted age. The Tech–Finance gap is $19,181 at 25–29, $27,303 at 40–44, and $28,430 at 60–64. After ages 45–49, the gap widens across each successive age group, from $17,872 at 45–49 to $28,430 at 60–64. Different job mixes and cohorts can help explain the uneven pattern.



Median earnings by five-year age group, pooled over income years 2022–2024.


The lines compare different people at different ages. They cannot show how one person’s wages will grow. Education, occupation mix, cohort differences, and who remains in full-time work can also shape the curves.

title: Tech Dominates the Forbes Rich List. Do Tech and Finance Careers Really Pay More?
section: Has the advantage changed since the 1970s?
text:
Has the advantage changed since the 1970s?
I measure each group’s annual premium as its weighted median divided by the Other median, minus one. This same-year ratio avoids comparing nominal dollars across decades. In 1975, Tech’s premium was 48.7% and Finance’s 27.3%. By 2024 they were 93.3% and 63.3%. The gap between their premiums grew from 21.4 to 30.0 percentage points. It fluctuated along the way; it did not widen every year.



Tech and Finance median earnings premiums relative to Other, income years 1975–2024.


The earlier Tech samples are smaller, and changes in occupational coding, income disclosure rules, and CPS weights limit exact comparisons over fifty years. The 2013 income observation uses the original 5/8 questionnaire in the 2014 ASEC redesign. These descriptive differences do not isolate the effect of choosing a career, let alone the effect of AI.

title: Tech Dominates the Forbes Rich List. Do Tech and Finance Careers Really Pay More?
section: What should a career chooser take away?
text:
What should a career chooser take away?
Tech and Finance workers in this full-time, full-year sample earn more at the median than the broad Other group, and the gap is already visible at ages 25–29. Tech leads Finance in the recent data and throughout the age profile. Their relative advantages are larger than in the 1970s, but the pattern is uneven. These group medians do not predict what any one person will earn.

Source and replication. Flood et al., IPUMS CPS: Version 13.0, ASEC extract 1. See the full replication guide, README, and analysis repository for definitions, sample counts, code, and results. The authenticated CPS microdata are kept outside the public repository.

title: Sunk Costs: Why Past Effort Should Not Decide Your Next Step
text:
“I’ve already put so much into this. I can’t stop now.”
We say it about a disappointing purchase, an unfinished project, or an investment that has gone wrong. Continuing seems to respect the money and effort already spent. Yet economics asks a surprisingly difficult question: if those resources cannot be recovered, why should they determine what we do next?

title: Sunk Costs: Why Past Effort Should Not Decide Your Next Step
section: What is a sunk cost?
text:
What is a sunk cost?
A sunk cost is a cost already incurred that cannot be recovered through the choices now available. It can involve money, time, or effort. The defining feature is irreversibility, not how large or painful the cost feels.
You have paid for a nonrefundable ticket, but halfway through, you realize you dislike the film. Whether you stay or leave, the ticket payment is gone. What you can still choose is how to spend the rest of the evening.
Staying cannot recover the payment. If another activity would be more enjoyable, staying only sacrifices more time. That forgone alternative is an opportunity cost: the value of the best option you give up. For more on this example, see OpenStax’s discussion of sunk costs.



The ticket is nonrefundable: staying or leaving cannot recover the $20. What remains yours to choose is the next hour.

title: Sunk Costs: Why Past Effort Should Not Decide Your Next Step
section: Why does ignoring it feel wrong?
text:
Why does ignoring it feel wrong?
We are taught to avoid waste and reward persistence. Leaving the cinema, abandoning a project, or changing direction can feel like admitting that our earlier judgment was wrong. Continuing lets us hope the original effort will eventually be justified.
The confusion is between two questions: “Was my original decision worthwhile?” and “Which choice is better now?” The first evaluates the past; the second guides the future. A bad answer to the first does not automatically make continuing the best answer to the second.
The sunk cost fallacy occurs when an unrecoverable past investment pushes us to continue even though the remaining benefits do not justify the remaining costs. Sunk costs themselves are ordinary; the fallacy is allowing them to distort the next decision.



Past spending is the same under either choice. Compare the consequences that today’s decision can still change.

title: Sunk Costs: Why Past Effort Should Not Decide Your Next Step
section: Three common misunderstandings
text:
Three common misunderstandings
“Everything I have already paid is sunk.” Not necessarily. A refundable deposit can still be recovered. Equipment may have resale value. Those recoverable amounts matter because today’s choice determines whether you receive them. What matters is recoverability, rather than simply whether payment happened earlier.
“Ignoring sunk costs means giving up.” No. Suppose finishing a project costs another $40 and produces $70 of benefits. Continuing adds $30 of value, regardless of the unrecoverable amount already spent. If the benefit were only $30, continuing would instead lose another $10. Assume stopping has no further payoff and these figures include all relevant future consequences.
“The past no longer matters.” Past experience can reveal whether a plan works, and previous spending affects the resources you still have. Use that information. Also include future exit penalties, switching costs, and the value of alternatives. Ignoring sunk costs means excluding an irreversible cost from the comparison, not erasing history or ignoring constraints.

title: Sunk Costs: Why Past Effort Should Not Decide Your Next Step
section: One example: waiting for a stock to recover
text:
One example: waiting for a stock to recover
An investor buys a share for $100; it is now worth $60. “I’ll sell when I break even” makes the purchase price a target, but does not explain why holding is attractive today.
The share still has $60 of sale value, so the asset is not entirely sunk. Holding means choosing to keep that $60 invested. The decision should compare future prospects, risk, alternatives, and relevant costs. A price decline alone proves neither that selling nor holding is best.






NoteOptional illustration: change the purchase price





This hypothetical example compares holding with selling for $60 and keeping cash for one year. It excludes dividends, interest, taxes, trading costs, and risk adjustment. Changing only the purchase price changes historical profit or loss, but not the expected advantage of holding over selling. Changing the expected future price can reverse that comparison.

title: Sunk Costs: Why Past Effort Should Not Decide Your Next Step
section: Why this matters outside investing
text:
Why this matters outside investing
The same reasoning helps us reconsider a study method, a business project, or how we spend an evening. Hours already spent cannot be reclaimed, but the next hour can still be used well. Before continuing, identify what is unrecoverable, compare the remaining options, and include what each option requires you to give up.
The lesson is not to quit sooner. It is to choose the next step for what it can achieve. Past effort deserves reflection; future effort needs a reason.

Source and illustration. Definition and movie example: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, §2.1, “Sunk Costs” (read the section). Numerical examples and the interactive illustration are hypothetical, not market data. The movie comic was created with AI assistance to illustrate the same principle. Editable article and widget: blog/posts/post1/; illustrations: images/blog1/ in the website repository. Rendering instructions are in its README.

title: One Policy, Two Mandates, Three Treasury Reactions
text: Higher interest rates can restrain inflation but weaken hiring; comparing the Fed’s policy cycle with labor-market conditions and Treasury yields reveals both this balancing act and its transmission across maturities.

title: One Policy, Two Mandates, Three Treasury Reactions
section: From public pages to comparable data
text:
From public pages to comparable data
I used rvest to extract yields from the U.S. Treasury, CPI and unemployment from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and policy records from the Federal Reserve. Its key value is extracting dates and decision text from FOMC statements, allowing yield changes to be matched to the days policy news reaches markets.
CPI inflation is the seasonally adjusted index’s twelve-month percentage change. Each yield’s announcement-day change is its difference from the previous trading observation, multiplied by 100 to convert percentage points into basis points. The sample contains 1,178 Treasury dates, 56 macro months, and 18 rate-change announcements, ending in September 2026 for yields and August for macro data.

Policy tightened after inflation surged, while unemployment stayed low. October 2025 CPI and unemployment observations are missing because of a lapse in appropriations.


The observed policy cycle is consistent with progress toward balancing inflation and employment, but not a completed or permanent success. Inflation fell sharply without a large rise in unemployment, then rebounded. Four stages show how the balance changed:

Tightening, 2022–2023: the policy midpoint rose above 5%. Inflation fell from its 9.0% peak to 3.3% by October 2023, while unemployment was 3.9%, close to its 4.0% starting level.
Holding high rates, 2023–2024: by August 2024, inflation had fallen to 2.6%, while unemployment reached 4.2%. Further disinflation coincided with a softer labor market.
Easing, 2024–2025: inflation generally stayed around 2.5–3%, while unemployment reached 4.4% in September 2025. The shift toward cuts was consistent with greater concern about employment.
Renewed tightening, 2026: inflation reached 4.2% in May and eased to 3.4% in August, with unemployment at 4.1%. Renewed price pressure provides context for September’s hike; its macroeconomic effects are outside this sample.

These patterns cannot isolate policy’s causal contribution. CPI tracks price pressure here; the Fed’s formal inflation goal uses PCE prices.

Treasury yields did not move uniformly across maturities: the short end reversed more visibly with the policy cycle, while long yields remained elevated. The 2-year yield peaked at 5.19% in 2023, above longer maturities. By October 2024, the 30-year again exceeded the 10-year and 2-year. During 2025, the 30-minus-2-year gap widened from 0.61 percentage points in January to 1.07 in October as shorter yields fell more. By September 2026, 10- and 30-year yields were still 5.01% and 5.34%, showing that earlier cuts had not ensured lasting relief in long-term financing costs.

Absolute announcement-day Treasury yield changes by maturity.


Announcement-day movements were larger at shorter maturities: median absolute changes were 7.0, 5.0, and 2.5 basis points for 2-, 10-, and 30-year yields. The 2-year yield is more closely tied to near-term policy expectations; longer yields also incorporate distant rates and compensation for long-term risk. This provides an interpretation of the maturity pattern, not proof that each announced decision caused the daily move. The sample includes only rate-changing meetings, and daily changes also contain other news.

title: One Policy, Two Mandates, Three Treasury Reactions
section: So, did the Fed pull it off?
text:
So, did the Fed pull it off?
The evidence suggests progress in balancing inflation and employment, alongside stronger announcement-day yield movements at shorter maturities. Inflation’s rebound shows why that balance requires reassessment rather than declaring victory after disinflation. For investors, the practical implication is to distinguish near-term yield sensitivity from long-bond price risk: smaller yield moves do not necessarily mean smaller price losses, because longer-duration bonds are more sensitive to a given yield change. For borrowers, a Fed cut alone is insufficient evidence that long-term financing has become cheaper; the relevant maturity’s market yield still matters.

Sources and reproducibility. U.S. Treasury daily par yields; Federal Reserve target-rate history, FOMC calendar, and policy statements; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI and unemployment tables. See the README, and the analysis repository. The analysis uses saved public-page snapshots and records source URLs and file fingerprints in the analysis repository’s results/ folder.

title: High Yields, Hot Currencies?
text: In a volatile world, investors may seek the predictable income of government bonds. Higher yields can make those bonds look more attractive. Overseas investors buying unhedged foreign bonds also need the local currency, potentially increasing demand for it. This raises a natural question: can more attractive government bond yields help strengthen a currency, or is the yield advantage over other countries what really matters? Exchange-rate losses can offset bond income, making this distinction important for international investors.

title: High Yields, Hot Currencies?
section: Do yields and currencies move together?
text:
Do yields and currencies move together?
First, do the country-level paths reveal a clear relationship? I combine OECD Financial Market yields with BIS broad nominal effective exchange rates (NEER) and BIS bilateral exchange rates for the United States, Japan, United Kingdom, Canada, and Switzerland, monthly from January 2017 through April 2026.
OECD’s long-term rate indicator represents benchmark ten-year government yields, in percent per year. NEER measures a currency against a trade-weighted basket: a rising index means appreciation, with 2020 averaging 100. BIS bilateral rates measure local currency units per US dollar; a falling number means the local currency strengthens against the dollar.






Figure 1: Each country’s yield (blue, left axis) and NEER (gold, right axis). All panels share the same axis ranges.



Figure 1 reveals no obvious common pattern. US yields and dollar strength sometimes move together, suggesting the proposed relationship. Japan often shows the opposite: yields rise while its currency weakens. Canada, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland show less consistent alignment. These paths cannot establish a general correlation, and dual-axis slopes depend on scaling. We therefore need to compare changes systematically.

title: High Yields, Hot Currencies?
section: Do rising domestic yields accompany appreciation?
text:
Do rising domestic yields accompany appreciation?
Next, does a rise in a country’s own yield coincide with currency appreciation over the same year? I calculate the twelve-month yield change, yt−yt−12y_t-y_{t-12}, in percentage points; a positive value means the bond now offers a higher yield. NEER appreciation, 100(Nt/Nt−12−1)100(N_t/N_{t-12}-1), measures the percentage strengthening or weakening against the currency basket over that year. Positive values mean appreciation. The transformations leave 100 monthly observations per country, January 2018–April 2026.






Figure 2: Twelve-month domestic yield changes versus NEER appreciation. Each dot is a month; lines summarize the relationship.



Figure 2 shows weak positive correlations in Canada (0.24), the United States (0.18), and Switzerland (0.12), but negative ones in Japan (-0.38) and Britain (-0.12). Rising domestic yields alone do not consistently accompany stronger currencies. Could investors instead respond to how yields compare with alternatives abroad? I next use US Treasuries as the benchmark.

title: High Yields, Hot Currencies?
section: Does the yield advantage over the US matter more?
text:
Does the yield advantage over the US matter more?
Does an improving yield advantage over US Treasuries align more closely with appreciation against the dollar? I calculate the domestic-minus-US yield spread and its twelve-month change; a positive change means the domestic yield becomes more attractive relative to the US yield. Dollar appreciation is 100(Et−12/Et−1)100(E_{t-12}/E_t-1), using monthly-average rates. Because EE is local currency per dollar, the ratio is reversed so that a stronger local currency produces a positive return.






Figure 3: Changes in the yield advantage over US Treasuries versus local currency appreciation against the dollar.



Figure 3 shows upward-sloping relationships for Japan (0.69), Canada (0.46), and Switzerland (0.26). The pattern is clearest in Japan, moderate in Canada, and weaker in Switzerland. Britain remains an exception, with a slight negative relationship (-0.13).
To compare absolute and relative yields more clearly, the table places their correlations with currency strength side by side, using the same measure of appreciation against the dollar and the same 100 months. Yield-spread changes show a stronger positive correlation in Japan and Canada, while Switzerland shifts from a negative to a positive relationship. Britain remains slightly negative. Overall, yield-spread changes are more positively associated with currency appreciation than domestic yield changes, but this positive relationship is not universal.

title: High Yields, Hot Currencies?
section: What is the answer for investors?
text:
What is the answer for investors?
More attractive domestic yields do not consistently accompany stronger currencies; the yield advantage abroad helps explain some country patterns, but supplies no universal rule. Domestic yield changes align weakly with appreciation in the US and Canada, while Japan and Britain show negative relationships. Relative yields reveal positive relationships in Japan, Canada, and Switzerland, yet Britain remains negative. Each country has its own pattern. Investors should therefore consider not only higher yields but also potential losses from exchange-rate movements and the costs of currency conversion or hedging.
These contemporaneous associations do not establish that yields caused capital inflows. Inflation expectations, policy surprises, risk premia, and hedging also matter.

Sources and replication. Data come from OECD Financial Market and BIS exchange-rate datasets. The R scripts for downloading, cleaning, and plotting the data, together with the archived data and replication instructions, are available in the GitHub repository. See the README to reproduce the figures and results.

title: Does the year change the parent–child income relationship?
text: Higher-income parents may afford better education, helping children obtain better-paying jobs. To explore this relationship, we use SQL to match parents and children and regression to estimate the relationship between their earnings. We also compare single-year estimates with estimates based on income averaged across several years to assess how sensitive our results are to income measurement.

title: Does the year change the parent–child income relationship?
section: How do we match parents and children?
text:
How do we match parents and children?
I use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics: the 2023 Parent Identification File, 1968–2023 Cross-Year Individual File, and 2017–2023 biennial Family Files. Earnings refer to 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022.
“Income” here means individual labor earnings, excluding farm and unincorporated-business income and pensions. Parental earnings combine the recorded mother’s and father’s earnings; child earnings are their own.
From the Parent Identification File, we select identifiers linking each child to their recorded mother and father. From the Cross-Year Individual File, we select original family ID, person number, current family ID, age, and household role for each survey year. From the Family Files, we select earnings for the household reference person and spouse. We join individual and family records by current family ID and survey year, assign earnings by household role, and match children to their parents using individual identifiers.
A wave is one interview round. Matching within the same wave links all three people in the same survey year: for example, the 2017 interviews reporting 2016 earnings.
In Python, sqlite3 executes SQL; pd.read_sql_query returns results as DataFrames.
-- 1. SELECT the identifiers and earnings to keep.
SELECT l.child_id68, l.child_pn, ch.wave,
       ch.earnings AS child_income,
       mo.earnings + fa.earnings AS parent_income
FROM links l
-- 2. JOIN each child using original family ID + person number.
JOIN personal ch
  ON ch.id68=l.child_id68 AND ch.pn=l.child_pn
-- 3. Match the recorded mother in the SAME survey wave.
JOIN personal mo
  ON mo.id68=l.mother_id68 AND mo.pn=l.mother_pn
 AND mo.wave=ch.wave
-- 4. Match the recorded father; never substitute a current spouse.
JOIN personal fa
  ON fa.id68=l.father_id68 AND fa.pn=l.father_pn
 AND fa.wave=ch.wave;
The table tracks sample selection. “Children” counts distinct people; “child–year records” counts one observation per child per income year. Thus, 411 children observed over four years contribute 1,644 records. Valid records require all three people aged 19–110 and nonmissing earnings. Positive child earnings and parental sums permit logarithms; one parent can earn zero.

title: Does the year change the parent–child income relationship?
section: Does the estimated relationship change by year?
text:
Does the estimated relationship change by year?
Estimate OLS without additional controls, where CC is child earnings and M+FM+F is parental earnings:
log⁡Cit=αt+βtlog⁡(Mit+Fit)+εit.\log C_{it}=\alpha_t+\beta_t\log(M_{it}+F_{it})+\varepsilon_{it}.
The intergenerational elasticity (IGE), βt\beta_t, measures the percentage difference in child earnings associated with 1% higher parental earnings. For the multi-year model, average earnings in levels before taking logs.






Figure 1: Same 411 children throughout; bars show 95% confidence intervals clustered by shared-parent networks.



All estimates show a positive association between parental and child earnings. The estimates for 2020, 2022, and averaged income are statistically significant at the 5% level. The IGE is 0.126 in 2020, 0.078 in 2022, and 0.117 using averaged income. The 2016 and 2018 estimates are positive, but their confidence intervals include zero. Single-year estimates can vary with temporary earnings shocks and career stages. Averaging can smooth temporary fluctuations, making income a better measure of longer-run earnings. Next, we explore how parents’ and children’s life-cycle earnings patterns can affect these estimates.

title: Does the year change the parent–child income relationship?
section: How could life-cycle bias enter?
text:
How could life-cycle bias enter?






Figure 2: Fixed groups based on 2017 interview ages. Parents’ lines show combined earnings, grouped by the father’s age. Dollars are nominal.



Median earnings rise in every child age group, while parental medians fall in both groups with fathers initially aged 55 or older. The youngest children rise from $31,750 to $58,250; parents in the oldest group fall from $62,250 to $34,279. The under-55 parent group rises overall. These patterns fit career progression and retirement.
A young worker’s earnings may understate later earning capacity, while older parents’ declining earnings may obscure earlier prosperity. Such age-dependent measurement can distort the IGE if people’s earnings trajectories differ; uniform proportional growth would only shift the intercept. Haider and Solon document this link between age and how well current earnings measure lifetime earnings.
Averaging spreads measurement across several career stages and reduces dependence on one unusually good or bad year. Here, it combines children’s earlier, lower earnings with later, higher earnings, and older parents’ earnings before and during their decline. The resulting IGE of 0.117 is less dependent on choosing 2018’s low estimate or 2020’s high one. It need not be the average of annual slopes.

title: Does the year change the parent–child income relationship?
section: Does ranking change the answer?
text:
Does ranking change the answer?
RichildR_i^{child} and RiparentR_i^{parent} represent the child’s and parents’ percentile positions within our sample. Rank child earnings and combined parental earnings separately, from lowest to highest. Equal earnings receive the average of their tied positions (midrank). Calculate:
Ri=100×midrank⁡i−0.5N,N=411.R_i=100\times\frac{\operatorname{midrank}_i-0.5}{N},\qquad N=411.
Higher values indicate a higher position in that generation’s earnings distribution. Then estimate:
Richild=a+bRiparent+ui.R_i^{child}=a+bR_i^{parent}+u_i.
With averaged earnings, b=0.238b=0.238: a ten-percentile-point parental advantage is associated with 2.38 percentile points in child rank. Annual slopes range from 0.147 to 0.193.
IGE measures percentage earnings gaps; ranks measure relative positions, limiting extreme amounts’ influence but discarding gap sizes. Neither is universally better: use IGE for earnings differences and ranks for relative mobility.

title: Does the year change the parent–child income relationship?
section: Takeaway
text:
Takeaway
Higher parental earnings are associated with higher child earnings. Using averaged income, the IGE of 0.117 means that 1% higher parental earnings are associated with approximately 0.117% higher child earnings. Averaged income can better reflect long-run earnings than single-year income by spanning career stages and reducing dependence on earnings at one age. The rank coefficient of 0.238 means that a ten-percentile-point parental earnings advantage is associated with a 2.38-percentile-point advantage in child earnings.

Sources and replication. PSID supplies the data; the project README documents variable definitions, data access, and how to reproduce the analysis.

title: How Can One Sample Tell Us About an Entire Population?
text: A city economist cannot interview every household before estimating monthly spending. Statistical inference measures uncertainty across samples. Here, you can draw households, build confidence intervals, and test a spending claim in a city whose true mean we know.

section: How certain is the estimate?
text:
How certain is the estimate?
Bootstrap estimates sampling uncertainty from one observed sample when the population distribution is unknown. Treat the sample as the population: draw n observations with replacement, calculate their mean, and repeat B times. title: How Can One Sample Tell Us About an Entire Population?
section: Is $3,000 a plausible mean?
text:
Is $3,000 a plausible mean?
A test statistic summarizes how far the sample result is from a claim, relative to sampling uncertainty. Test H₀: μ = μ₀ against H₁: μ ≠ μ₀, initially μ₀ = $3,000. Here, t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n): x̄ is the sample mean and s its standard deviation. The estimated standard error, s/√n, measures typical variation in sample means. Thus, t expresses the observed gap in standard-error units.

Figures 5 and 6 use the same null distribution: Figure 5 sets rejection thresholds using α; Figure 6 measures extremeness using the observed |t|. Its orange tails show simulated outcomes at least this extreme in either direction. This area estimates the p-value: the probability, assuming H₀ and the model are true, of a statistic at least this extreme. A small total orange area means our result is unusual under H₀. Reject when p ≤ α; change μ₀ or α to explore the decision. The p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true; failure to reject does not establish equality.

title: How Can One Sample Tell Us About an Entire Population?
section: What one sample can tell us
text:
What one sample can tell us
Bootstrap estimates uncertainty from one sample: resample with replacement, plot the means, and use their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for a 95% interval. The default interval is $2,796–$3,305. 95% confidence describes repeated-sample coverage: approximately 95% of intervals should contain μ; here, 941/1,000 do. Hypothesis testing assesses evidence against a claim by comparing the observed statistic with simulations under H₀. Rejection regions contain values deemed too extreme at the chosen α. The p-value is the probability under H₀ and the model of a statistic at least as extreme. Here, p = 0.686 exceeds 0.05, so we do not reject the $3,000 claim.
